memory_leads.lead: Shipboard electrical availability is an actor/system chain spanning engineering crew and technical management, generator prime movers and alternators, switchboards/buses and protection, distribution to essential and nonessential loads, plus emergency or external power sources; installed nameplate capacity is not the same as usable resilient power.

Generation availability is stateful: installed sets may be running, stopped, under maintenance, failed, starting, synchronized or held in reserve. Available spinning or startable capacity therefore differs from total installed generator capacity.

Generator synchronization and load sharing form a coordination layer. Having multiple healthy generators does not guarantee stable supply if they cannot be connected, paralleled or share changing load as intended.

Switchboards, bus sections, ties and distribution paths define electrical failure domains. Redundant consumers or generators can still be lost together when they depend on a common bus, protection path or distribution component.

Load shedding is a controlled degraded-state mechanism: when generation is insufficient or unstable, lower-priority loads may be disconnected to preserve essential propulsion, steering, pumps, navigation or safety functions rather than allowing an uncontrolled total collapse.

A blackout is a system-state transition, not merely one failed component. Loss of the main electrical network can simultaneously remove pumps, controls, auxiliaries, lighting, navigation support and other functions even when the main propulsion machinery itself is mechanically undamaged.

Blackout recovery is a sequence: establish an independent starting/control source, restore generation, energize buses, reintroduce essential loads and then nonessential loads while avoiding another overload or protection trip. Recovery time can therefore be materially longer than generator start time alone.

Emergency power is a separate limited-capability island intended to keep selected essential services available after loss of main power; its presence does not mean normal propulsion, cargo or hotel capability is restored.

UPS, batteries or dedicated control-power supplies can bridge short interruptions for selected electronics and controls, creating different endurance windows across systems during a main-power disturbance.

Power quality—voltage, frequency and waveform stability at a structural level—matters separately from simple energized/de-energized status because sensitive drives, electronics and control systems can trip or misbehave under degraded supply even while a bus remains live.

Large changing loads can create dispatch and transient constraints: starting pumps, compressors, thrusters or cargo machinery may require generation margin and sequencing, so nominal steady-state capacity can overstate what can be restored or operated simultaneously.

Shore power creates an external electrical interface with compatibility, connection, isolation, switching and port-supply readiness states. Availability at berth depends on both ship and shore sides rather than on the vessel installation alone.

Battery or hybrid-electric storage introduces state-of-charge, charge/discharge power, thermal/safety management and integration states that can support peak shaving, reserve or propulsion/auxiliary functions, but exact architectures and capabilities are deferred.

P027 common-mode OT failure should explicitly include shared electrical supply: independent controllers, sensors or communication nodes may still fail together when their power distribution is not independent.

P026 degraded-navigation logic is refined because bridge equipment may have unequal backup-power endurance; the information stack can degrade in stages after a broader electrical disturbance rather than disappearing all at once.

Operational availability should distinguish partial electrical degradation, controlled load shedding, blackout, emergency-power operation and full restoration. These states have different implications for safe navigation, cargo operations, port readiness and off-hire.

Energy-efficiency and decarbonization technology can increase electrical coupling among propulsion, hotel, cargo and storage systems; evaluation should therefore include resilience and recovery topology as well as nominal fuel or emissions performance.
Generic redundancy and common-mode failure were already captured in P027; P028 retains only the electrical generation/distribution topology that creates those shared failure domains.

General machinery maintenance and vessel off-hire effects belong to earlier technical coverage; P028 adds the electrical availability and restoration state chain rather than another component-maintenance catalog.

reviewed_no_specific_memory.reason: Blind memory supports generic generation/distribution states but cannot establish vessel-specific architecture, ratings or protection design.
Specific blackout causes, timing and consequences require engine-room records or casualty Evidence.
Carriage, endurance, connection and safety requirements vary by regime, system and date and require claim-scoped Evidence.
Project identity, technical capability and current status require source-first Evidence.

stop_reason: The electrical availability chain is populated from generation readiness and synchronization through bus/distribution failure domains, load shedding, blackout/restart, emergency/UPS states, power quality, large-load sequencing and shore/battery interfaces. Further recall becomes equipment-, rating-, rule-, casualty-, project- or vessel-specific.
truth_boundary: Memory-only orientation; no vessel electrical topology, equipment rating, blackout cause, restoration duration, regulatory requirement, battery/shore-power project capability or current electrical condition is verified.
